descriptionChirho: Qal stative: to be physically heavy, weighty, or burdensome in a literal sense, describing hands, yoke, famine, battle, or other tangible things.
Nifal participial and finite forms: to be honored, esteemed, or noble; used substantively as 'nobles, honored ones' — the passive counterpart of Piel 'honor'.
Nifal imperfect/cohortative/infinitive: to be glorified or to get glory, predominantly said of God showing His glory through mighty acts.
Piel active: to honor, respect, or esteem a person (parents, elders, God), corresponding to Arabic كَرَّمَ, Korean 공경하다, Swahili -heshimu.
Piel active with God as object: to glorify, give glory to God or His name, corresponding to Arabic مَجَّدَ, Korean 영화롭게 하다, Swahili -tukuza.
Hifil causative: to make heavy, burden, or harden (especially Pharaoh's heart); also to make a yoke or hand heavy upon someone — Arabic أَثْقَلَ, Korean 완고하게 하다.
Piel or Qal used specifically for hardening the heart (making it unresponsive), as in the Exodus narrative — a metaphorical extension of 'make heavy'.
Hifil used with a positive honorific sense: to bring honor to, to make glorious (a land, a people) — distinct from the negative 'make heavy/harden'.
Adjectival or stative use: to be rich, wealthy, or abounding in possessions — an extension of 'heavy' to mean 'substantial in goods'.
Qal imperfect: to be a burden to someone, to weigh down upon others — a figurative extension of physical heaviness to interpersonal relations.
Hitpael reflexive: to make oneself heavy, i.e. to multiply, increase, or boast/glorify oneself.
Qal imperfect used in a jussive/optative sense: 'let [the LORD] be glorified' or 'may [God's name] be honored' — stative with glory semantics rather than physical weight.
